title: Duplicate payment requests create duplicate business records
description: Prevent duplicate payment records by implementing idempotency keys, the outbox pattern, and compensating transactions in payment processing systems.

data.text: A customer reports being charged twice for a single order. Your database shows two payment records with different IDs but the same order reference. The payment gateway confirms it received and processed two requests. The root cause is a missing idempotency mechanism: when the client retried after a network timeout, the server treated it as a new payment instead of a duplicate.

items: Client times out waiting for the payment response and retries with a new request ID
Server processes the payment but crashes before returning the response
Network retries at the gateway or load balancer level resend the request
User double-clicks the Pay button because the UI does not disable immediately
A webhook from the payment provider is processed twice due to redelivery

terms.definition: A unique identifier provided by the client that the server uses to detect duplicate requests.
The risk of charging a customer twice for the same transaction without their knowledge.
Storing payment events in an outbox table within the same database transaction as the payment record, then publishing them reliably.
A reverse operation that undoes the effects of a previous transaction, used to correct duplicates or failures.
An external service (Stripe, PayPal, etc.) that processes payment authorizations and captures.

items: Client generates a unique idempotency key (e.g., UUID) for every payment attempt
Server stores the idempotency key with the payment result before calling the gateway
On duplicate requests, the server returns the stored result instead of reprocessing
Use database unique constraints on (order_id, status) to prevent duplicate records at the data layer
Implement the outbox pattern to ensure payment events are published exactly once

cards.title: Idempotency key in request
cards.description: Client sends a unique key; server deduplicates using a lookup table.
cons: Server must persist keys with TTL

cards.title: Database unique constraint
cards.description: Enforce uniqueness at the database level with a composite key.
pros: Cannot be bypassed by application bugs
cons: Less flexible for complex business rules

cards.title: Outbox pattern
cards.description: Store payment events in the same transaction as the payment record.

cards.title: Compensating refund
cards.description: Detect duplicates asynchronously and issue a refund automatically.

    A[Client: Create Payment] --> B[Generate Idempotency Key]

data.title: Payments require idempotency by default
data.text: Any payment endpoint that does not accept and enforce an idempotency key is a liability. When a customer is charged twice, the cost is not just the refund: it is trust, regulatory exposure, and payment processor fees.

items.question: Should the client or server generate the idempotency key?
items.answer: The client should generate it. If the server generates it, the client cannot safely retry because it does not know the key for the original request.

items.question: How long should I keep idempotency keys?
items.answer: Keep them for at least the refund window plus a buffer (e.g., 90 days). After that, archive them to cold storage.

items.question: What if the payment gateway itself duplicates the charge?
items.answer: Use the gateway's idempotency key feature (Stripe supports this natively). Combine it with your own idempotency key for defense in depth.

data.title: Add idempotency to a payment API
data.description: Find a payment or checkout endpoint in your codebase. Add an idempotency key requirement and duplicate detection logic.
steps: Identify the payment creation endpoint and its current input schema
Add an IdempotencyKey field to the request model
Create a Payments table with a unique constraint on IdempotencyKey
Implement the duplicate-check logic before calling the payment gateway
Write a test that sends the same request twice and asserts the second returns the same result
data.expectedOutcome: You should have a payment endpoint that safely handles retries without creating duplicate charges or records.

data.title: Summary
points: Duplicate payment requests are expected in distributed systems; handle them by design
Require client-generated idempotency keys on all payment endpoints
Enforce uniqueness at the database level with a unique constraint
Use the outbox pattern to ensure payment events are published reliably
data.takeaway: In payment systems, idempotency is not a feature; it is a requirement. Build it into the API contract from the first version.
